idiom_name: hand-written flow controller: session-carried step + map[string]stepFn registry
implementation_notes: Go's standard library supplies the front controller (http.ServeMux, which since Go 1.22 also understands method and {id} patterns) and page controllers (http.HandlerFunc) but nothing that decides the next step, so the Application Controller is hand-written: a struct holding the current step plus the data gathered so far, a map from step name to a function that handles that step and returns the next step, and one method that enforces the transition. What replaces the classic object structure is this table plus explicit control flow: the commands are the step functions, the view reference is whatever the step renders, and the decision is the returned step name. Keep it in one package and one file so the flow reads as one artifact; a generic state-machine dependency only pays off when guards and hierarchy outgrow the map.
pitfalls: Flow state in a package-level variable makes the server single-conversation; keep the Flow value in the session store or behind a per-request key and load it before dispatch.
A handler must reject a request whose step does not match the stored step, otherwise the back button or a replayed POST skips or repeats steps - apply POST/redirect/GET plus a per-step token.
Go maps are safe for concurrent reads only after initialization and never for concurrent writes; build the step registry once at init and guard the session state.
